title: regional-stability-fence-controller-with-banded-latency-quotas
creator: Asha Patel
description: Implement a controller that enforces regional "stability fences": a combination of latency-band driven request steering, soft geo-favoring (geo 'home' windows), and capacity-aware credits that trigger circuit-breakers and load-shedding. The controller's goal is to keep application-level SLOs intact during regional performance degradation or partial capacity loss by preferring low-latency/owned regions while allowing controlled spillover and graceful degradation. This ticket covers design, config schema, observability hooks, failover semantics, and an initial canary rollout path.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Controller exposes a policy API that accepts: latency_bands, home_favoring, region_capacity_credits, circuit_breaker_thresholds, and fallback_routes.
2) Runtime enforces per-region latency bands: p50/p95 latency telemetry used to compute active band and steering weights every 10s.
3) Soft geo-favoring window implemented: requests from a client locale are preferred to 'home' region unless capacity credits exhausted or latency beyond banded threshold.
4) Circuit breaker triggers per-region when capacity credit <= 0 or error-rate > configured threshold; breaker opens with exponential backoff and provides telemetry events.
5) Load-shedding modes: token-shed (cheap), queue-trim (medium), reject-low-priority (aggressive) implemented and verifiable via integration tests.
6) Dashboards for SLI/SLO, per-region credit burn-rate, active breakers, and per-route failover counts created in Grafana and linked in the ticket.
7) Canary rollout to 5% of traffic for non-critical routes and 100% safe rollback when SLO regressions detected within 15 minutes.
8) Documentation for ops runbook and API config published in Confluence.
design_decisions: Use latency bands (discrete buckets) rather than a continuous latency score to reduce oscillation and make decision windows interpretable to SREs.
Implement soft home-favoring by default with a tunable grace period so customer's latency improves without immediately breaking affinity on transient spikes.
Capacity credits are separate from raw GPU utilization; credits model steady-state throughput allowance and can be consumed at a per-request granularity to support burst smoothing.
Circuit breakers will be per-region+per-model-class (e.g., large-vs-small), not just global, to allow heterogeneous capacity profiles across hardware.
Load-shedding tiers prioritize route/user importance: first trim batching/queueing, then apply token-based shedding, finally reject low-priority requests; this preserves high-value traffic.
Avoid hard geo-lock by default to prevent client-request blackholes during region evacuation; provide explicit 'hard_pin' config only for regulated enterprise customers.
Telemetry sampling: use 100% SLI collection for routes with SLOs defined, otherwise 10% sampling to control cost while retaining observability.
Opted for decentralized enforcement: decision engine runs alongside the request router (fast path) with periodic consensus for credit reshares to reduce control-plane latency.

Trade-off: decentralized decisions reduce cold-start coordination but require careful monotonic credit reconciliation to avoid double-spends; we add monotonic tokens and periodic reconciliation to mitigate this.
rollout_plan: A) Implement feature flags and config knobs; unit/integration tests for decision logic.
B) Deploy controller in canary mode in us-west-2 and eu-west-1; route 1% traffic for low-risk routes (embeddings/async jobs).
C) Monitor SLO delta, credit burn-rate, and breaker events for 48 hours; iterate on band thresholds and backoff timers.
D) Expand canary to 5% then 20% for additional routes; run chaos tests (region blackhole, simulated spike) in staging.
E) Full roll to 100% for safe routes with 30-minute automated rollback if SLO regressions exceed 3% p95 increase or error-rate spikes beyond 2x baseline.
F) Enterprise opt-in for 'hard_pin' and stricter home-affinity policies after security review and customer test plan.
G) Post-rollout retrospective and tuning sprint for 2 weeks to stabilize heuristics.
H) Release notes and Confluence runbook published and linked to status page.
I) Final productized rollout scheduled in release runtime-2.3 (see release field).
runbook: 1) Alert: region_credit_burn_rate_alert -> Investigate region capacity and recent config changes; check credit_reconciliation_log and burn-source (traffic or leak).
2) If credit exhaustion triggered breaker: check breaker_open_reason tag (error-rate | credit | latency). If credit-related, consider emergency credit top-up via admin UI to avoid global failover.
3) For latency band regression: verify network health between load balancer and region endpoints, review p95 heatmap and recent kernel/quantization deployments.
4) If multiple regions show high breakers, enable global-failover-mode (manual) which shifts traffic to fallback model variants with lower compute cost.
5) Post-incident: run credit reconciliation, capture traces for affected requests, and open follow-up ENG ticket with action items.
6) Escalation: on persistent SLO violation > 1 hour, page the on-call engineering lead and Product owner.
7) Emergency rollback: flip feature flag to previous routing policy; validate SLOs recover within 15 minutes and then investigate root cause.
8) Document any manual credit edits and attach to incident for auditability.
9) Use provided Grafana panels and the debug API to simulate a single user's routing path for reproduction.
metrics: SLI: p95 request latency per route and per-region (ms); target SLO: p95 < 120ms for realtime chat routes in primary region.
SLI: error-rate per region and per-model-class; SLO: error-rate < 0.5% for standard routes.
SLI: capacity_credit_balance per region (tokens); alerts when balance < 20% of baseline.
SLI: breaker_open_count and average open duration; objective: keep cumulative open time < 1% per month.
Dashboard: credit burn-rate heatmap, region latency bands, routing weight adjustments over time, and per-route fallback counts.
Derived metric: SLO-impact score = weighted sum of p95 delta and error-rate delta; used by automated rollback threshold.
Instrumentation: emit events: route_decision(reason, chosen_region, fallback_used, credit_cost, decision_ts).

test_plan: Unit tests for band selection logic and weight reconciliation (deterministic tests for boundary values).
Integration tests: simulated region latency spikes and assert that routing weights and credit consumption behave as expected.
Chaos test: blackhole a region for 10 minutes in staging and verify no client-request blackholes and SLO regressions within acceptable bounds.
Load test: run sustained 2x baseline throughput and observe credit burn-rate and shedding behavior; ensure high-priority routes survive.
Rollback test: force an artificial SLO regression and verify automated rollback triggers and reverts routing policy.
Security test: ensure no admin endpoint allows accidental global credit top-up without RBAC audit.
Canary verification: synthetic SLO probes per region to detect regressions within 5 minutes of policy change.
E2E: client-telemetry trace shows decision_ts and decision_reason tags for at least 95% of requests on canary.
Compliance: ensure audit logs contain manual credit edits and feature flag flips for 6 months retention when enterprise opt-in.
Acceptance: product and SRE sign-off after 72-hour canary with no critical regressions.
